name: Wei Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wei, I'm 27. I'm a junior buyer at Kestrel Motor Factors, which supplies car parts to independent garages: brake pads, filters, batteries, wiper blades, that kind of thing. I live with my partner Sana, who works at a bank branch in town. I finished school, did a couple of years on the parts counter, and moved into buying last year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in at half eight, look at what the garages ordered yesterday, and phone the suppliers to restock. I still use the paper catalogue for some of the older brands, which my boss Derek finds funny. Then I check deliveries against the orders, which takes ages because the part numbers are long. I like knowing my parts. What I don't like is the new supplier website we're supposed to use, because it logs me out every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's sensible, not everything needs to change. I'd say it at the counter to the lads and they'd agree. I wouldn't post anything online, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad, because I've never touched one of those AI things. I know I'm slow with new systems. If I don't have to learn them, I've got time to get better at the job the normal way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just keep going. Get faster at checking deliveries, maybe learn the brake ranges properly so Derek doesn't have to check them. Sana and I would keep saving; my grandad left me some money, so with that we're about a year and a half covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this world that would still bother you about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Garages closing, I suppose. Electric cars need fewer brake pads and no oil filters, so in ten years we sell less anyway. That's the slow thing nobody talks about at Kestrel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Derek push any new tools on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Derek would make me use the supplier website, but I can live with that. A website is not the same as a robot buyer.

say: I'd say it's **sensible** that not everything needs to change.
I'd say it at the **parts counter**, not online.
think: I'd be **glad**, since I've never used AI and I'm slow with new systems.
I'd have time to get better at the job **the normal way**.
do: Learn the **brake ranges** properly so Derek doesn't have to check them.
Keep saving with Sana; with grandad's money we have **eighteen months** covered.
S0.quote: Electric cars need fewer brake pads and no oil filters, so in ten years we sell less anyway.
fieldNote: He sees **electric cars** as the real slow threat to his trade, not AI.
His savings and **inheritance** make him secure in this world.
He openly prefers the **familiar**: phone, paper catalogue, and slow learning.

steps.text: Learn the brake pad ranges well enough to work unchecked
Keep saving with Sana alongside grandad's inheritance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see. Every few years there's some new thing that's meant to change everything. At the counter I'd say the garages still want a person on the phone who knows their car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be worried. Buying is literally on your list, and I'm the junior who doesn't use any of it. Derek's not going to keep the slow one if a computer can reorder filters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask to go back on the parts counter, where I talk to mechanics all day. I'd keep my head down and save. I'm not going to rush into a course for something that might not happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like when you've ordered the wrong part and the garage is waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try learning the AI ordering tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't, really. I know I should. But I'd rather go back to the counter than be bad at a computer in front of everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sana at the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Sana works at the bank answering people and checking forms, so both of us are on that list. That's the bit that actually scares me.

fieldNote: He expects his buying job to **shrink** and himself to go first.

He realises **both household jobs** are thinking work, which raises his worry.

steps.text: Ask Derek for a move back to the parts counter
Keep saving each month and spend nothing big

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should put the brakes on. I'd tell the garage owners they're next, because AI can diagnose faults too. I still wouldn't post anything, but I'd talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my buying job is gone by 2028, and my partner Sana's job at the bank is probably gone too. The counter might last a bit, but if a garage can order online from an AI, they don't need me on the phone either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no holiday, no new car. I'd move to the counter or the warehouse, anything hands-on. Maybe I'd ask my uncle about his tyre-fitting business, because that's real hands-on work till the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would tyre fitting last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years in the tyre shop, maybe more. Robots fitting tyres sounds far off, but you said 2031. After that I've no idea, and that's what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If both of you lost work, how would you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have a year and a half of savings, and grandad's money is part of that. I'd rather not touch it, but we would. And my family would help; that's what they're for.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and someone should put the **brakes** on.
I'd warn garage owners that AI can **diagnose faults** too.
think: My buying job is **gone by 2028**, and Sana's bank job probably too.
Even the counter goes if garages **order from an AI**.
do: Cut back straight away: **no holiday**, no new car.
Ask my uncle about work at his **tyre-fitting** business.
S2.quote: My buying job is gone by 2028, and my partner Sana's job at the bank is probably gone too.
fieldNote: He expects **both household jobs** to go, which pushes him to alarm.
His plan is hands-on work at his **uncle's tyre business**, buying time to 2031.
He'd lean on **family and savings**, but hates touching grandad's money.

steps.text: Cancel this year's holiday and the new car
Ask his uncle for work at the tyre-fitting business
Lean on family if both jobs go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so people shouldn't panic. I'd tell the lads at the counter to watch the news. I'd probably say it'll be slower than they say, like everything is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same end for me. The buying job goes around 2031. But I'd have five years, and I'd think I can wait a couple before doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Kestrel for now and keep saving. In a couple of years, if it looks real, I'd join my uncle at the tyre shop and learn the trade. I don't want to jump too early and look stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not as bad. There's a bit of time to sort things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Waiting a couple of years with five on the clock: isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fair. I'm not a jumper. But I would start saving harder from now, more than we do, so whatever I end up doing, we've got a bigger cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Sana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd think about it more than me. She's better with change. She'd probably push me to do something sooner.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so people **shouldn't panic**.
I'd tell the counter lads it'll probably be **slower** than they say.

With five years, I'd think I can **wait a couple** before acting.

Join my uncle's **tyre shop** in a couple of years if it looks real.

fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the job**, but his instinct is to **wait**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty of things could change. I'd say the same at the counter: don't lose sleep over 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by then I'd be somewhere else anyway, maybe running the counter or at the tyre shop. I'd be 37. Something will turn up, there are always parts jobs around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much at first. Keep working, keep saving, maybe buy a house with Sana. In five years I'd look again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but it doesn't feel close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You also mentioned electric cars shrinking the business. Doesn't that add up over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. Electric cars and AI together will shrink the parts trade, but I can't do anything about either of them today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could waiting catch you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. That's the trouble with me, I wait. I'd tell myself to check every year.

I'd tell the counter lads **not to lose sleep** over 2036.

There are always **parts jobs** around here, so something will turn up.

fieldNote: He expects his **income** to hold because local parts jobs are plentiful.
His habit is to **wait**, and he names it as a risk himself.
He links AI to the slower threat of **electric cars** shrinking parts sales.

steps.text: Keep buying at Kestrel and review options in five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sana and I would both be hit at once and I'd have no time to learn anything. What would help is proper hands-on apprenticeships for grown adults, paid, and some help with the mortgage if both earners lose work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the garages. If AI can tell people what's wrong with their car, the small garages I supply might go too, and then nobody needs a parts buyer at all.

headlineQuote: If AI can tell people what's wrong with their car, the small garages I supply might go too, and then nobody needs a parts buyer at all.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** junior car parts buyer at Kestrel, living with Sana, a bank worker.
He has never used AI and prefers the **phone and paper catalogue**.
With savings and an **inheritance**, he's calm in the plateau but alarmed when AGI is near.
His fallback is hands-on work at his **uncle's tyre shop**.
His instinct is to **wait and see**, and he knows it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and Sana would both be hit with no time to learn anything.
whatWouldHelp: Paid adult **apprenticeships** and **mortgage help** if both earners lose work.
